items.title: docs(eval): publish the v0.2.0 benchmark results
items.body:
## What changed

Publishes `EVAL_RESULTS_0_2_0.md` — the v0.2.0 campaign results — plus the two reporting scripts it cites (`stats.py`, `sensitivity.py`) and the regenerated `results.json`.

162 runs: 3 arms × 18 tasks × 3 repetitions, Django 6.0.7 at `e2a4246`, worker model `claude-haiku-4-5`.

## Why

The final PR of the stack. Everything below it landed the fixes, the harness, the isolation enforcement and the methodology; this reports what the campaign measured.

## Benchmark failure class

**agentlens passes every pre-registered falsification condition against both controls.**

| Condition | Threshold | Measured |
|---|---|---|
| Cost ratio vs baseline | < 0.5 | **0.4365** |
| Cost ratio vs linerange | < 0.7 | **0.5145** |
| Accuracy vs baseline | not > 0.05 below | +0.0641 above |
| Accuracy vs linerange | not > 0.05 below | +0.0451 above |
| Losses vs baseline | ≤ 4 of 18 | 3 |
| Losses vs linerange | ≤ 6 of 18 | 2 |

Three findings run *against* the tool, and the document gives them at least as much prominence as the verdict.

**1. The accuracy advantage is mostly a rubric artefact I introduced.** The localization prompt says *"return only the repo-relative address(es) you would edit"*. **`address` is agentlens's own vocabulary** — its output is `path#Symbol`, so it satisfies symbol-level gold for free, while a control arm reasonably answers `django/core/handlers/base.py` and scores zero. METHODOLOGY §5.2 explicitly forbids requiring agentlens's syntax; the *matcher* obeys that, the *prompt* did not, which is why fixing the matcher never caught it.

Re-scoring localization so naming the correct file counts:

| Localization recall | Pre-registered | File-only |
|---|---|---|
| agentlens | 0.444 | 1.000 |
| baseline | 0.167 | 1.000 |
| linerange | 0.194 | 0.944 |

Every arm found the right file essentially every time — the gap was notation, not navigation. The accuracy delta falls from **+0.064 to +0.022** against baseline. Four of 18 tasks currently measure nothing. The cost claim survives the same correction (0.3614 / 0.5809), and moves in opposite directions against the two controls, which is what an artefact rather than a thumb on the scale looks like.

The pre-registered rubric stays authoritative for the verdict; `sensitivity.py` reproduces the bound.

**2. agentlens malformed 7.6% of its calls; both controls malformed 0%.** Invented flags (`--expand`, `--include-strings`, `-t`) and outlines passed where a symbol address is required. `stats.py` separates usage errors from legitimate empty results — `rg` exiting 1 on no match is not a defect and neither is `agentlens find` doing the same — so the comparison is fair rather than inflated.

**3. agentlens loses on navigation**: 2.0 calls to the first gold address against 1.5 for both controls, and it had the widest accuracy spread across repetitions of any arm.

The v0.1.0 comparison is published for traceability but explicitly **not** for inference: that campaign ran a different model *family* (`gpt-5.6-sol`), so every cross-campaign delta confounds tool version with model. The previously quoted 5.9× figure should not be carried forward.

## Verification

```
uv run --directory evals/harness python validate_protocol.py
protocol validated: 162 fresh runs, schedule/order, caps, hashes, and determinism

uv run --directory evals/harness python detect_leaks.py
checked 162 completed runs
MEMORISATION (capped): 2 run(s) — r1-agentlens-L05, r3-baseline-L01
by arm: {'agentlens': 1, 'baseline': 1, 'linerange': 0}

uv run --directory evals/harness python -m unittest test_harness test_gate
Ran 66 tests — OK

./scripts/ci.sh --fast   # gate passed
```

**Zero isolation breaches across 162 runs.** The two memorisation flags both hit the call cap, and are retained and reported rather than re-rolled — re-running a capped run in the author's own arm is indistinguishable from re-rolling until the tool looks better. One is in Arm A and one in Arm B.

## Token-cost impact

None — reporting only.

## Deviations

The campaign ran 3 repetitions, not the pre-registered 5, recorded in §7 and in PR #32. Stopped on cost grounds before any grading. Every interval here rests on three points, so the IQRs are crude; agentlens's own accuracy ranged 0.571 / 0.624 / 0.746 across the three.

items.title: Correct the metric and fold wording on the benchmark results page
items.body:
The benchmark results page says:

> The results are reported regarding mean accuracy and standard deviation across all folds for all sessions and subjects.

Two corrections:

**Not always accuracy.** [`MotorImagery.scoring`](https://github.com/NeuroTechX/moabb/blob/4be37764cda18bfa7245a7f63be041a3f5cf1d75/moabb/paradigms/motor_imagery.py#L302-L307) returns `roc_auc` at exactly two classes and `accuracy` above — so **Left vs Right Hand** and **Right Hand vs Feet** are ROC-AUC, **All classes** is accuracy.

**Not across folds.** `WithinSessionEvaluation` [averages folds](https://github.com/NeuroTechX/moabb/blob/4be37764cda18bfa7245a7f63be041a3f5cf1d75/moabb/evaluations/base.py#L922-L926) within `(subject, session, pipeline)` before returning, so BNCI2014_001 gives 90 fits but 18 rows and the reported spread is between `(subject, session)` pairs.

Found while reproducing the `TS+LR` BNCI2014_001 cell — mean 71.9732 against the published 71.97, with 15.46 recovered as the population SD over those 18 rows.

Docs only, no code changes.

items.title: docs(benchmarks): record first evaluation baseline
items.body:
## Summary

Records the first reviewed baseline for the multiclass evaluation scaling benchmark family (#121), following the same pattern as the affine augmentation (#117-#118) and dataset discovery (#119-#120) baselines.

**Harness commit:** exact SHA `658a6bcc6b943a1f9e232be51149b2d52d1a08d2` (`commit_info.dirty: false`), captured with a clean working tree before any documentation edit.

**Capture command:**
```bash
OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 MKL_NUM_THREADS=1 \
uv run --group benchmark pytest benchmarks/benchmark_evaluation.py \
  --benchmark-warmup=on --benchmark-min-rounds=20 \
  --benchmark-storage=file:///tmp/improcv-evaluation-benchmark-storage \
  --benchmark-save=evaluation-baseline
```

**Preflight:** AC power (79%, charging), load averages ~2.6/3.9/4.6 on a 12-core machine (ordinary background load, no build/test/container process) -- a first preflight attempt found the machine on battery, and a second found a transient macOS background-maintenance CPU spike (`softwareupdated`/`mobileassetd`) right after plugging in; both delayed the capture until conditions settled.

**Result:** 16 benchmark entries, groups `evaluation-confusion-matrix:3` / `evaluation-classification-metrics:3` / `evaluation-roc-auc-macro:5` / `evaluation-average-precision-macro:5`, across sample scaling (1,000/10,000/100,000, fixed 10 classes) and ranking class scaling (3/10/100, fixed 10,000 samples), all `rounds >= 20`. Compact, stats-only saved run -- `stats.data` confirmed absent from every entry. JSON SHA-256: `5d1beb309d6f8d94d60dc955514b1ccc9dd626100d9d9239d08899349b923f2f`, identical before and after copying into the repo.

**Scaling (this machine, this run only):** all four operations' medians increased monotonically with sample count, and both ranking operations' medians increased monotonically with class count. Each 10x sample-count step produced ~8.3x-10.7x median growth across the four operations; the ranking class-count steps (3.33x and 10x class growth) produced ~3.1x-3.2x and ~9.9x-10.3x median growth respectively -- all reported as "approximately proportional over the measured range," never as a proven asymptotic complexity claim from three points. Label-based workflows ran two to three orders of magnitude faster than ranking workflows at matching sample counts, as expected (ranking does one binary computation per class plus its own score-matrix copy/validation).

**Stability:** relative IQR stayed under 7% for all 16 entries. Two `classification_metrics` cases (1,000 and 10,000 samples) showed notably higher coefficient of variation (28.7%, 35.9%) than the rest, traced via `min`/`max` to a small number of high-round-count rounds affected by ordinary OS scheduling jitter (max/median ratios of 6.5x/10.6x) -- the same signature already documented and accepted (without re-running or discarding) in the affine baseline's own high-CV case. Median/IQR (this project's primary statistics) stayed low and unremarkable for both.

Full tables, environment details, and limitations are in the reviewed report:
- Compact JSON: [`benchmarks/results/2026-08-02-evaluation-baseline.json`](benchmarks/results/2026-08-02-evaluation-baseline.json)
- Reviewed report: [`benchmarks/results/2026-08-02-evaluation-baseline.md`](benchmarks/results/2026-08-02-evaluation-baseline.md)

**Documentation correction:** `benchmarks/README.md`'s "Stable local run" section previously showed an example that ran all of `benchmarks/` but saved the result as `augmentation-baseline` -- ambiguous now that there are three families. Both the compact-baseline and full-data-capture examples are now family-specific (`FAMILY=evaluation`/`FAMILY=augmentation` variables, saved-run name matching the family), while noting that running the whole `benchmarks/` directory remains valid for a quick local review, just not how a committed baseline is produced.

## Verification performed

- Correctness/collection smoke (`--benchmark-disable -s`, before capture): `16 passed`; diagnostic setup times recorded (label datasets all <1ms; ranking datasets <6ms each except the first, which took 1.895s of first-use/allocation noise from the process's first `default_rng` call, outside the timed region) -- never treated as benchmark results.
- Normal suite: `uv run pytest` -> **4191 passed, 6 skipped** (unchanged).
- Full benchmark smoke: `uv run --group benchmark pytest benchmarks/ --benchmark-disable` -> **42 passed**.
- `ruff check .` / `ruff format --check .` / `pyright`: all clean.
- Build + packaging: `uv build` + `twine check` both PASSED; wheel unaffected (still excludes `benchmarks/`, 258,413 bytes); sdist grew from 2,127,408 to 2,138,945 bytes (+11,537 bytes, consistent with the new 37,943-byte JSON + 18,930-byte Markdown after compression) and includes both new files alongside the untouched affine/discovery baselines.
- Final diff before commit: `M CHANGELOG.md`, `M benchmarks/README.md`, `M benchmarks/results/README.md`, `?? benchmarks/results/2026-08-02-evaluation-baseline.json`, `?? benchmarks/results/2026-08-02-evaluation-baseline.md` -- exactly as scoped; `benchmark_evaluation.py`, `conftest.py`, other harnesses/results, CI, and packaging config are all untouched.

## Test plan

- [x] `uv run pytest` unaffected (4191 passed, 6 skipped)
- [x] `uv run --group benchmark pytest benchmarks/ --benchmark-disable` -> 42 passed
- [x] JSON integrity verified programmatically (SHA, dirty:false, 16 entries, groups 3/3/5/5, no stats.data, no temp paths, correct metadata, no duplicate 10000x10 scenario)
- [x] SHA-256 identical between `/tmp` capture and repo copy
- [x] Lint/format/type-check clean
- [x] Packaging (wheel/sdist) verified with twine

**Not merging this PR** -- please review before merge.

items.title: docs(plan): record the resolved speed picture
items.body:
Completes the plan's Part 2 with what today actually established. The earlier update captured the first measurement; four corrections followed, and the corrections are the useful part.

## The benchmarks were lying in two different ways

Fixed and shipped in #7403. Discarding the result let Perry eliminate the loop; and even with it consumed, `fibonacci(FIB_N)` is loop-invariant, so it hoists out and runs **once** — checksum correct, `TOTAL` zero.

| benchmark | was reported | actually |
|---|---|---|
| `bench_fibonacci` | ~240× faster | **2.5× faster** |
| `bench_bitwise` | ∞ faster | **20.4× SLOWER** |

## The fast path already exists

`bench_bitwise`'s hot loop has **no runtime helper calls at all** — 4 `frem` per iteration, `4 × bl _fmod`, 1754 profile samples. But `expr/binary.rs:588` already emits guarded `srem` with the IEEE `-0` correction. The gap is the analysis, reduced to one line (#7404):

```ts
let a = 12345678; … a % 1000            // srem — fires
let a = 12345678; … a % 1000; a = a + 1 // frem — lost
```

Four wrong hypotheses about that subsystem are recorded so they aren't retried, along with why a careless widening is dangerous: it returns silently wrong integer arithmetic that `===` tests cannot see.

## A measured negative result

`js_array_grow`'s HOLE-init loop is **already vectorised** (6 `stp` in the baseline), so the `slice::fill` rewrite proposed for #7396 measures nothing. The contrary reading came from grepping a symbol absent from a stripped binary — `grep -c` returns 0 whether or not the pattern exists.

## Method notes strengthened

Third instance today of a check that could not fail, and a new one worth its own line: **a fix that compiles, passes every correctness test, and changes no emitted instruction is a fix to the wrong site.** The guarded `srem` I wrote for #7404 passed the entire `-0` edge-case table and emitted zero `srem`.


<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->
## Summary by CodeRabbit

* **Documentation**
  * Updated performance documentation with corrected benchmark results and validation details.
  * Documented that `bench_bitwise` is significantly slower than Node due to repeated modulo calculations.
  * Clarified findings around integer analysis, array growth, loop optimization, and store performance.
  * Added notes on rejected optimization hypotheses and improved measurement methodology.
<!-- end of auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->

items.title: Benchmark: gemini36flash — complete run, scored, and recorded in benchmarking-results.md
items.body:
Third model measured in the multi-model benchmark, after `luna` run 6 and `glm52`. The run is **complete and scored**; results are appended to `docs/benchmarking-results.md`.

## Result

Rebased to the 97 reachable entries, same scorer and same denominator as the other two rows.

| Metric | `gemini36flash` | `luna` run 6 | `glm52` |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Recall** | **57/97 = 58.8%** | 69/97 = 71.1% | 65/97 = 67.0% |
| Recall, category-blind | 67/97 = 69.1% | 77/97 = 79.4% | 77/97 = 79.4% |
| **Localization** (±15) | **73/97 = 75.3%** | 86/97 = 88.7% | 83/97 = 85.6% |
| Localization, blind | 89/97 = 91.8% | 93/97 = 95.9% | 91/97 = 93.8% |
| File-level | 96/97 = 99.0% | 97/97 = 100% | 97/97 = 100% |
| **Precision proxy**, aware | **16.5%** (47/285) | 12.5% (69/553) | 7.8% (70/892) |
| Findings | 285 | 553 | 892 |
| Distinct lines cited | 1,181 | 3,597 | 4,577 |
| Mean / max trace steps | 4.56 / 13 | 8.74 / 51 | 6.64 / 38 |
| Tokens | 9,381,580 | 9,618,943 | 9,668,297 |
| Cost | $24.85 | $4.37 | $17.01 |
| Runtime | 32m12s at C=8 | 13m04s at C=32 | ~18.5 min at C=32 |

`ai-llm-agency` scored **1/4** — the first non-zero on that class by any model here; both peers scored 0/4. `misconfiguration` at 3/17 is the weakest per-class figure in the file.

Single-variable against run 6: Stage 0.5's manifest is **identical** to it — same 865 lane ids, same 541-lane hunt set, same target files, zero lanes with differing assigned classes — so Stage 2's model is the only difference.

## Execution

541/541 hunt lanes, 865 consumption entries (541 hunt + 324 skip), 865 unique `lane_id`, **0 duplicates, 0 `failed: true`**, `exit_code 0`, `degraded: false`, `blocked_reads: 0`, 1,082 calls = exactly 2 per lane. Guards **226 passed, 0 failed**.

The run took three launches: container reclamation at 143 lanes; a 429 storm at `HUNT_CONCURRENCY=16` that lost 53 lanes; then a clean C=8 resume that finished 125/125 with 0 retries. The 53 lanes were correctly re-queued and all completed, so the scored artifact covers every lane. Program spend was 11,597,180 tokens across the three launches.

## Two corrections to the plan, both from measurement

**§9.4 — Gemini rate limiting.** The section previously said Gemini enforces spend-based limits (~$10/10 min) that stall "without a 429". Wrong on both counts, and it misdirected my own diagnosis. The binding limit is ordinary **TPM**, surfacing as a plain `429 status code (no body)`. Console figures at tier 1: **1,000 RPM / 2,000,000 TPM / 10,000 RPD**, with 28-day peaks of 232 RPM / 1.63M TPM / 2.36K RPD. That 1.63M peak is **82% of ceiling**, reached at C=16, against the runbook's standing 40–50% target. Per-unit throughput here is ~102k TPM — six times `luna`'s ~16k at the same effort — which puts the derived concurrency at 8.8, hence **8, a ceiling rather than a starting point**. Raising it to 16 was my decision and is the proximate cause of the lost lanes; that is stated in the row and in the archive, not buried.

Also recorded: `gemini31pro` at **25 RPM / 250 RPD** cannot complete 1,082 calls in a day at any concurrency.

**§9.7 — Gemini thinking tokens are billed but not counted.** `total_tokens` exceeds `prompt_tokens + completion_tokens`; the gap is thinking, which `models.json` says the vendor bills as output. On the final pass: 1,587,996 + 36,141 = 1,624,137 against `total_tokens` 1,963,904 — **339,767 unaccounted**. `costUsd()` prices `completion_tokens` alone, so `usage-v2.json` under-reports Gemini spend. The output column in the results file is visible output **plus** thinking, which is what makes it comparable to the `luna` and `glm52` columns.

## Stage 0 ran at default reasoning effort, Stage 2 at high

`stage0-recon/src/llm-probe.ts` hardcodes output caps of 500 and 5,000 rather than reading `outputTokenCap()`, while still spreading `samplingParams()`. Measured against the live endpoint with the verbatim prompts and real corpus files:

| probe | cap | effort | finish_reason | thinking | outcome |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| tool-calling (`routes/chat.ts`) | 500 | default | `stop` | — | parses |
| tool-calling (`routes/chat.ts`) | 500 | **high** | **`length`** | ~357 | truncated, `JSON.parse` fails |
| category (real arch summary) | 5000 | default | `stop` | 2,212 | parses |
| category (real arch summary) | 5000 | **high** | **`length`** | 2,427 | truncated |

On failure `markDegraded()` fires and Stage 0 falls back to deterministic analysis — a *different recon* that would later read as a model result. `llm-probe.ts:68` prints `[LLM OK]` **before** `JSON.parse`, so a truncated body still logs OK; `meta.json → degraded` is the only trustworthy signal. Default effort also matches run 6, whose Stage 0/0.5 came from run 3 and predate `reasoning_effort` existing. Stage 0 here recorded `degraded: false`.

## What this PR touches

- `docs/benchmarking-results.md` — **append only.** Every `luna` and `glm52` cell is byte-identical to `main`, §2.1 and §2.2 unchanged, rules and method sections unchanged; verified cell by cell rather than by eye. The sole removal is `gemini36flash`'s own row from §4 Pending, now recorded in §1.
- `docs/protocols/benchmark-run-plan.md` — §1 scope, §6 concurrency and rate limits, §9.4 rewritten, §9.7 added. Includes a merge of `main` resolving two conflicts with the `glm52` session; neither side's content is dropped.
- `results/eval-history/scanner.jsonl` — one line appended (16 → 17). Report regenerated from the history files.
- `tools/scanner/runs/gemini36flash/` — stage artifacts.

The run archive, including all three launch logs, is in the answer-key repo at `runs/2026-08-02T16-38Z__stage2-v2-perfile-trace-loop__gemini36flash__2a4bf04/`.

Aggregate metrics only — nothing here pairs a challenge identifier with a file, a line, or a found/not-found status.

items.title: docs(eval): post-fix validation telemetry report (smoke scope)
items.body:
## Linked Issue Or Context

- Reports on #387 / #388 (fixed in #402), and records evidence behind #406, #407 (#409), #408.
- Docs/data only. No source changes.

## Summary

Adds `benchmarks/results/2026-07-31-validation-telemetry.md` plus the raw
double-arm JSONL under `benchmarks/results/2026-07-31-smoke/`.

This is **not** a re-run of the 2026-07-12 ablation, and it deliberately draws no
pass-rate conclusion. It answers a prior question: **is the "multi-layer
validation never intercepted anything" finding itself trustworthy?**

Answer: partly not — a substantial part of it was an **observability artifact**.

### The load-bearing evidence

A deterministic probe — zero LLM spend, identical input, through the real
`runFrontAgentTask` entry point the harness uses:

| | pre-fix (`develop` @ db42301) | post-fix (#402) |
|---|---|---|
| `validation_failed` | **0** | **1** (`syntax_validity`) |
| bad file on disk | **yes** (40 B) | **no** |
| task error | `Syntax errors found in …` | `Pre-write validation failed: …` |
| `step_failed` | 1 | 1 |

`step_failed` is 1 in **both**. The check was running and failing all along — it
just emitted no event and left the file on disk. Pre-fix, `validation_failed` had
no emit site anywhere in the repo, so it could not have been anything but 0.

### Three limitations stated up front in the report

1. **`validation_failed` was not a pure interception signal in this run.** The
   numbers were produced on #402's first implementation (`543b791`), where the
   event compounded pre-execution structural blocks, real content interceptions,
   and **pure tool failures** (`validateAfterExecution` returns `results: []` on
   `success === false`). Fixed later in `1a54e25`; the report classifies every
   event in this run rather than quoting a raw count.
2. **n=5 per arm.** No pass-rate conclusion is drawn.
3. **Bad files still reach disk.** Both `full`-arm failures were `TS1127` — model
   prose written into `.ts`/`.tsx`. Feeding those exact artifacts to the guard
   returns `pass: true` (#406). The interception bottleneck is now checker
   strength, not the executor pipeline this PR series fixed.

### Numbers

| | full | ablation |
|---|---|---|
| passed | 3/5 | 2/5 |
| `validation_failed` (old composite) | 0 | 2 |
| — real content interceptions | 0 | 0 |
| — classification undecided (structural block **or** pure tool failure) | 0 | 2 |
| `rollback_started` | 0 | 0 |
| wall time | 27.2 min | 28.6 min |
| LLM calls (failures) | 34 (0) | 39 (0) |
| tokens in/out | 112,648 / 137,363 | 98,101 / 160,163 |

### Full 30-task run: not run

Not blocked by quota — blocked by wall time, so per instruction it was not forced.
Extrapolation = July's per-arm 27-task total x **30/27 task scaling** x **that
metric's own measured ratio** (this run / July's same 5 tasks). Ratios measured
per arm and per metric — `full` 1.109 / 1.251 / 0.988 (time / in / out),
`ablation` 0.886 / 1.372 / 1.162:

| | full | ablation | both |
|---|---|---|---|
| 30-task wall time | ~135 min | ~114 min | **~4.2 h** |
| input tokens | ~547K | ~440K | ~987K |
| output tokens | ~670K | ~759K | ~1.43M |

Cost stays **~$10 in order of magnitude**. An earlier draft multiplied time by
two factors and tokens by one, and reused `full`'s time ratio as a universal
token ratio; inputs came out ~30% low. Every input is recomputable from the two
committed JSONL pairs. Backend
availability verified (`claude` CLI v2.1.220, probe `is_error: false`, 73 calls
this run with 0 failures). Preconditions recommended before spending it are in
§6 of the report.

**The two ablation-arm events are deliberately left unclassified.** The report's
first draft called them pre-execution structural blocks; that contradicts the
error string it quotes elsewhere (`Cannot apply patch: file not found in
context:`, whose only producer is `executor-skills.ts:242`, thrown *during* step
execution). The two candidate classifications invert the conclusion under
`1a54e25`'s rule, and this run's JSONL kept only event counts — so the report
states it cannot be decided from committed data. Real content interceptions are
0 either way.

### Comparability against July

Verified at the July baseline commit `51fd4bb` rather than assumed. Same task
set, fixture, and model. Two genuine differences are documented in §5: the
`ablation` arm's semantics changed once #392 made `checks` effective, and #402
adds pre-write blocking. #407 degrades both arms and July identically, so it is
**not** an arm-biasing confound.

### Self-correction recorded in the report

I initially misattributed the ablation failures to #407 based on an error message
naming `claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022`, and filed an incorrect root-cause issue. That
model name is fabricated by `formatRunError` from resolved config and has nothing
to do with the failure site; the real error was
`Cannot apply patch: file not found in context: …`. #407 carries a correction
notice, and the true cause is #408. The report keeps this on the record because
the fabricated `provider`/`model`/`baseURL` triple is precisely what makes the
wrong conclusion look well-evidenced.

## Impact Scope

- `benchmarks/results/` only — one Markdown report and two JSONL files.
- No source, config, or workflow changes.

## GitNexus Impact Summary

- Risk level: LOW
- Critical skeleton changes: no — `benchmarks/results/` matches no critical contract rule; this is a documentation and data artifact.
- GitNexus impact: `detect_changes --scope compare --base-ref develop` reports 4 files / 15 symbols, **0 affected execution flows**, risk low; all symbols are Markdown headings in the new report, and `query`/`impact` show no code symbol reachable from these paths.
- Verification: `pnpm quality:precommit` exit 0 (turbo 25/25, workflows 34/34); no executable surface touched.

## Verification

- `pnpm quality:precommit` — exit 0, turbo 25/25 tasks, `test:workflows` 34/34.
- Raw JSONL committed alongside the report so every number is recomputable:
  `benchmarks/results/2026-07-31-smoke/{full,ablation}.jsonl`.
- The before/after probe is reproducible without LLM spend; its construction is
  described in §2 of the report.

## Checklist

items.title: docs: postmortem — why the chain loses to one agent, + 4 corrections [OPERATOR-PR]
items.body:
A four-agent evidence re-read (one on Fable) of the replay run tree, the
same-week single-agent control, and the chain source. Adds
`POSTMORTEM-2026-08-11.md`, corrects four things #321 got wrong, and rebuilds
the README's central table around the matched comparison.

## The hypothesis we most wanted tested is REFUTED

The chain does **not** degrade the dev's spec. In the bench arm there is no PM,
SM or contract — the dev's story **is** the raw problem statement, byte-shared
with the control through one template (`swebench_adapter.py:2193`, "one string,
four arms"). The chain loses on what it adds *around* an identical spec.

## Why it loses — five mechanisms, largest first

1. **It slices the dev's horizon.** Every attempt is a fresh sandbox capped at
   **1,800 s** (`runner.py:68`) while the arm clock is 5,400 s. The control's
   **winning** `exstruct-113` run took **1,807 s — longer than any chain attempt
   is allowed to live**. `vyper-4801`'s three attempts each died at the cap with
   `files_touched: []`: 6,341 s and $13.50 for **zero completed dev
   conversations**. The chain is not short of iterations — it buys *more* (2,058
   tool calls vs 1,169). The constraint is **continuity**.
2. **Its gates emit signals the dev cannot decode.** `exstruct-113`'s retry
   prompt contains `Summary: tests not green after run` directly above a tail
   reading `11 passed in 0.82s`, with no reason. Two retries were spent replaying
   an identical disagreement; the other two died to infra. Final diff: 0
   production bytes, $8.83. The control resolved it.
3. **Its verdict layer runs at chance.** P(resolved | green) = 58%,
   P(resolved | blocked) = 50%, base rate 56%.
4. **Its workspace corrupts its own evidence.** On `canvasapi-716` the reviewer
   called the production fix correct, demanded one more test, and the dev's edits
   hit `[Errno 13] Permission denied` on the 0444-locked file — the chain
   demanded, forbade, then punished the absence of the same edit.
5. **The tax is the dev loop re-executing itself**, not the extra personas:
   dev $76.82 of $81.00; 40 fresh conversations for 18 instances, 9 eaten whole
   by infrastructure, 34.6 M fresh input tokens vs the control's 6.4 M.

The identity `score = capability − tax + selection` is incomplete: capability is
not a constant the chain taxes, it is a function of
`(model, task, horizon_slice, policy, environment)`, and shipped work carries a
verdict-recall multiplier.

## Four corrections to #321

- **`line-bot-981` was NOT the dev's gitlink surgery.** That row's trajectories
  contain **no dev git plumbing at all** — only a chain `worktree_create`. It is
  a **workspace-preparation** defect. `tox-3931` *is* dev-side. A prompting fix
  would not have closed the second hole.
- **The arms are not budget-matched, and `swebench_adapter.py:4831` claims they
  are.** Iteration caps match (600); per-conversation wall clock does not
  (1,800 vs 5,400). Undisclosed asymmetry, biased **in the chain's favour**.
- **`exstruct-113` as "not machinery-attributable" is too kind** — it is a
  feedback-channel failure, a category the criterion does not model.
- **The 56% headline omits the operational number.** Three of the ten resolves
  ended in blocked states that would never merge. **Under live-chain semantics
  the factory is 7/18 = 39%.**

## The oracle is unenforced *and* often vacuous

`gate_enforced` is `false` on all 18 rows, yet authoring sits on the critical
path before the dev's first call. **7 of 18 oracle files contain zero asserts** —
the persona mandates HTTP-only tests with no app imports, and 7 of these repos
are libraries with no HTTP surface, so the author correctly emits a pure
`pytest.skip`. This **inverts the obvious fix**: enabling the gate would have
blocked 7 rows, 3 of which resolved — roughly 10/18 → 7/18.

## Verification

Docs-only: **0 Python files touched**. Full suite `-n 4` shows the same 5
acceptance-oracle failures as the `origin/main` baseline measured under identical
conditions — the documented contention class; they pass 70/70 in isolation.

items.title: fix(#514): gold-blind LoCoMo ID selection + corrected full re-run
items.body:
Closes #514

## The defect

`tests/benchmarks/scenarios/external_base.py` consulted the answer key when collapsing retrieved turns to result IDs:

```python
matching = [cid for cid in candidate_ids if cid in relevant_ids]
chosen_ids = matching if matching else candidate_ids[:1]
```

`candidate_ids` was `[session_id, turn_id]` (both id spaces lived in one map).

- **LongMemEval-S** annotates ground truth at session granularity, and the session ID was always element 0, so the gold-matching branch and the `candidate_ids[:1]` fallback emitted the same ID. Benign.
- **LoCoMo** annotates ground truth at turn granularity. A gold turn emitted its unique `turn_id` and kept its own rank slot; every non-gold turn collapsed into one shared `session_id` slot. Gold was lifted, and Recall@K / MRR with it.

Measured over the full 1986-question corpus: **20 retrieved turns became 13.245 rank slots on average** (`locomo_20260708.json`), against **19.916** after the fix (`locomo_20260807.json`). Issue #511's critique estimated ~11.9 from a sample; 13.245 is the full-corpus figure.

## The fix

Rank one consistent unit per dataset — turn IDs for LoCoMo, session IDs for LongMemEval-S — resolved from dataset metadata *before* retrieval runs, with gold-blind first-occurrence dedup.

- Each dataset adapter now declares `metadata["ground_truth_unit"]`; `tests/benchmarks/datasets.ground_truth_unit()` maps dataset names as the fallback. Neither path reads `relevant_ids`.
- `_session_key_map` is split into `_session_key_map` + `_turn_key_map`, so `run()` has no per-record granularity choice left to make.
- The collapse is `collapse_to_ranking_unit(retrieved_keys, unit_map)` — **no answer-key parameter exists**, so gold-awareness cannot reappear inside it without changing the signature.
- Unit granularity is documented in the report: a `ranking_unit` block in the JSON and a `**Ranking unit:** turn (gold-blind, first occurrence wins)` header line plus a Notes entry in the Markdown. Artifacts predating the fix render as `unrecorded (pre-#514 artifact)` rather than claiming a unit they never used.

## Corrected numbers

**LoCoMo lexical, full 1986 questions, `--sample stride --seed 0`** (`locomo_20260807.json`, macOS 26.5.2 arm64 / Python 3.12.13 / redis-py 8.x / Redis DB 11, 21.8 min):

| Metric | Corrected | Pre-#514 | Δ |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Recall@1 | 0.2981 | 0.2986 | −0.0005 |
| Recall@5 | 0.5302 | 0.5534 | −0.0232 |
| Recall@10 | 0.6017 | 0.6400 | −0.0383 |
| MRR | 0.4005 | 0.4124 | −0.0119 |

4-category leaderboard-parity slice (n=1540): 0.2877 / 0.5130 / 0.5877 / 0.3875 (was 0.2883 / 0.5390 / 0.6260 / 0.3991).

Lower on every metric, as expected. R@1 moves least: the compression mostly changed *how far down* gold could fall, not whether it was rank 0.

The superseded run stays committed as `locomo_20260708.json`; only the `locomo_latest` pointer moves.

**LongMemEval-S is unaffected — verified two ways.** Structurally, by a test asserting the corrected collapse is byte-identical to the reproduced legacy rule for every session-ID answer key. Empirically, by a full 500-question lexical re-run under the corrected harness (`longmemeval_s_20260807.json`): Recall@1 0.8560 / Recall@5 0.9520 / Recall@10 0.9780 / MRR 0.8987, **identical on all 500 questions individually** and per category, with only the latency fields differing. `longmemeval_s_latest` still points at the published `20260630` run.

## Not re-run

LoCoMo **hybrid**, **graph**, and **judged** arms still carry pre-correction scoring — hybrid/graph need a full embedding pass over 1.19M records, judged needs API keys. They stay published for continuity and are labelled pre-#514 on the docs site, in `docs/benchmarks.md`, and in the CHANGELOG. The docs' lexical-vs-hybrid comparison now explicitly reads the two pre-#514 rows against each other, which is the like-for-like pair.

## Tests

New `tests/benchmarks/test_gold_blind_scoring.py` (37 tests):

- `TestGoldBlindIdSelection` — `test_collapse_signature_cannot_see_the_answer_key`, `test_turn_ranking_is_one_slot_per_record`, `test_legacy_rule_moved_with_the_answer_key` (baseline: the old rule *was* gold-sensitive), `test_turn_ranking_identical_for_every_answer_key` (6 keys incl. withheld), `test_shuffling_the_answer_key_cannot_change_the_ranking`, `test_legacy_rule_compressed_slots_and_lifted_gold`, `test_unmapped_key_scores_as_an_honest_miss`
- `TestLongMemEvalUnaffected` — `test_single_session_matches_legacy`, `test_many_interleaved_sessions_match_legacy`, `test_turn_ids_can_never_collide_with_session_ids`, `test_scenario_ranks_sessions_end_to_end`
- `TestRankingUnitResolution` — adapter declarations, `test_unit_resolution_ignores_relevant_ids`, `test_locomo_scenario_ranks_turn_ids_end_to_end`, `test_locomo_scenario_ranking_survives_a_withheld_answer_key` (end-to-end: withheld and decoyed answer keys produce the identical ranked list)
- `TestRankingUnitInReport` — the unit reaches the JSON, the Markdown header, and degrades honestly for old artifacts

Plus `test_gen_benchmark_pages.py::test_no_broken_symlinks_under_results` — the two dangling `*_latest*` symlinks (`locomo_latest_graph`, `locomo_latest_ext-heuristic`, targets never committed) are removed and cannot come back silently.

`test_harness.py::TestLoCoMoParityRegression::test_lexical_parity_slice_is_1540_qa` is re-pinned to the corrected parity numbers, with the old values named in its docstring.

## Verification

- Editable install resolves to this worktree; `.[dev,embeddings,benchmark,docs]`; Python 3.12.13.
- Full suite, `POPOTO_TEST_DB=12`: **2450 passed, 30 skipped, 4 failed**. The 4 are `tests/test_pytest_plugin.py` DB-isolation assertions that hard-code DB 15; they pass on the default DB (`33 passed`). Not regressions.
- `mkdocs build --strict`: passes. Generated LoCoMo pages carry the corrected numbers, the ranking-unit header, and the correction notice.
- `black --check` clean on every file touched.
- Benchmarks ran on Redis DB 11 (`POPOTO_BENCH_DB=11`) to stay clear of the default bench DB 14; both runs swept clean at teardown.

## Docs claims affected

- `/benchmarks/results/locomo_lexical/` — numbers replaced, correction admonition added.
- `/benchmarks/results/` Overview — one-line correction notice above the LoCoMo section; MEMTIER anchor now cites 0.2981; cat-5 caveat labelled corrected.
- `/benchmarks/results/locomo_hybrid/` — new "scored before the #514 correction" admonition.
- `docs/benchmarks.md` — correction info box, corrected tables, pre-#514 rows kept and labelled, cat-5 figures updated.

The claim "Popoto lexical LoCoMo Recall@1 sits competitively in the MEMTIER 0.10–0.30 retrieval band" survives at 0.2981. (Whether the *band itself* is a defensible frame is #511's question, not this PR's.)

items.title: release: v0.126.1 — ship the corrected Zig binary-size claim
items.body:
No compiler changes. This exists to get a correction out of the repo and into users' binaries: `machin guide` had been telling every agent that machin beats Zig on static binary size, and **it does not**.

```
zig 0.15.2    873,760 B as-produced ->   15,760 B stripped  [static]
zig 0.16.0  3,594,056 B as-produced ->  503,256 B stripped  [static]
machin                                   14,544 B stripped  [dynamic]
machin --static                         940,000 B           [static]
```

Zig's **fully static** binary is ~16 kB — about the size of machin's *dynamic* one, needing nothing on the target — and **~60× smaller than machin's own `--static` build**. machin's size win is over **Rust, not Zig**. The guide catalog is compiled into the binary, so a release is the only way that correction reaches anyone.

Also records the second-machine verification that caught it (#588) and the manual bench workflow that ran it (#586, #587).

Version bumped in all four guarded/unguarded places: `guide.go`, README badge, `SPEC.md`, `CHANGELOG.md`.

Full suite green — `ok machin 251.725s`.

**One honest note:** an earlier full-suite run failed with four TLS/socket tests reporting `connection refused` (the MFL TLS server never started). Not reproducible — the same tests pass individually, together, and on `main`, and the diff at that point was a version string plus three docs. Treated as a flake, but recorded rather than quietly re-run until green.

items.title: docs(plans): PLAN-0103 — Step 6 record, six ACs closed, three corrections carried
items.body:
Brings PLAN-0103 into agreement with the code after Step 6 shipped in #1138. Six ACs closed in substance still read `[ ]` on disk, and Step 6 carried no execution record.

Authored by the in-harness `plan-drafter` from a Code dispatch (ADR-009 D1). Code verified the fact-pack on disk **before** dispatching and re-verified every drafter-originated citation after — which is what produced the two findings below.

## Ticked

AC-1, AC-2, AC-3, AC-4, AC-5, AC-7 — each with an evidence block citing artifacts by path/line rather than restating them.

## AC-6 deliberately NOT ticked

Verifying the fact-pack rather than relaying it found the "closed in substance" claim false for this one.

AC-6's own wording requires the per-system env-parse tests to exclude "the persona-key variable **if SD-4 introduces one**". SD-4 did introduce one — `UI_DEMO_PERSONA_KEYS` (ruling (b), s218), made a browser-served raw-key store by the s224 credential ruling. So that parenthetical is a live obligation, not a conditional.

- **Substance holds:** no committed file carries raw key values. Fleet's `published.env:88-90` states the variable's deliberate absence and why; `docker-compose.yml:69` is a bare host pass-through; `README.md:115-140` documents provisioning; `detect-secrets` green.
- **The guard does not exist:** no test anywhere asserts `UI_DEMO_PERSONA_KEYS` is absent from any committed file — the only two test files naming it *consume* the setting. And `test_ac4_no_secret_is_committed` reads only `oct-energy`'s env, because `_DEPLOY` is pinned there (`test_published_compose.py:59`); that module's own comment records the narrowing as temporary "pending the next step", which shipped in #1114/#1116.

Net: fleet and procurement are unguarded against exactly this AC's named secrets, and fleet is the profile that introduced the raw-key variable. Recorded as a partial record so it gets closed as **code**, never ticked as prose.

## Three corrections, classified per CLAUDE.md §6

**1. AC-7 — `was an error`.** The AC's own middle clause said `appr-fleet-manager-wirat` "approves within tier". The engine refuses him — `tier_role_mismatch … routed to 'appr-owner'` — because the DOA ladder routes the hero repair's amount to the owner tier.

It was false *when written*, not overtaken: `procedures.yaml` last changed 2026-07-29 and its tier block earlier still, both before the PLAN was drafted 2026-08-09 — and the YAML's own comment at `:282-286` already said the ฿48,000 breakdown "clears ฿30,000 and lands on the OWNER's desk". Nobody ran it. Same failure family as Lesson #0041.

The AC still closes, because what shipped is **strictly stronger** than what it asked for: two refusals from two *different* governance mechanisms (separation of duties; DOA tier routing) plus one grant. A module showing only a granted approval passes with SoD deleted; one showing only an SoD refusal passes with the ladder flattened.

**2. AC-1 — `superseded by new info`.** Its literal closure condition reads "Grep = 0 matches"; a raw grep now returns 1 — comment prose in `app.js:36` explaining what replaced the constant. The shipped oracle is comment-stripped and deliberately stronger. The corrected condition ("no live-code mention") is recorded with both surviving comment sites named, so a future session running the literal grep does not read a 1-match result as an unclosed AC.

**3. ADR-0037's status — `superseded by new info`.** The PLAN called it "Proposed" in four places; it has been **Accepted** since 2026-08-10 (s218). Refreshed at the Related-ADRs line, Step 4's gate map (gate satisfied, not pending), SD-1's ruling stamp, and the References entry. The dated 2026-08-10 rulings-round paragraph keeps its original wording as a historical snapshot, matching how earlier rounds' superseded statements were left intact.

## Step 6 recorded

Under its step, in Step 10's style: PR #1138, Cray's two typed s224 rulings (layout A; credential (a)) restated, the served-to-the-browser key posture cited to its committed rationale, the boot-refusal guards including the crossed pair, and `view-monitor.js`'s `isPublished()` count going 0 → 1 against the zero Step 3 recorded.

Three items from the session-224 closeout are **attributed rather than adopted** — the pre-test non-vacuity probes, the browser display-honesty probe, and the test-count delta were not re-verified by this edit. Laundering relayed claims into PLAN-level fact is the mechanism Lesson #0041 documents.

## Scope

No ruling, scope, step, or SD slot changed. `Status:` stays `Draft` — AC-6, AC-10 and AC-11 remain open. One file changed.

## Verification

Full offline gate on the committed tree `ae39f56`, captured before pushing so `git diff --stat HEAD` was empty and the gated tree is provably the pushed tree:

- `pytest tests/` — **4025 passed, 8 skipped** in 478.31s. Identical to the pre-edit baseline, which is the check that matters here: prose is under test in this repo and pre-commit does not run pytest.
- `mypy --strict services/` — no issues in 134 source files.
- `ruff check .` / `ruff format --check .` — clean on the committed tree, verified via `git archive HEAD` into a scratch dir. (A bare local `ruff check .` reports one S108 in `.claude/benchmark-results/`, an **untracked** scratch file absent from git and from CI.)

The Axis-B `goal-evaluator` judged the edit adversarially from disk: **J1–J4 PASS**, J5 pending on this merge.

## Note for a follow-up, not part of this PR

`.claude/launch.json` is untracked but **not** covered by `.gitignore`, and it names `UI_DEMO_PERSONA_KEYS` — verified via `git check-ignore` (rc=1). A `git add -A` would stage it. The keys it holds are synthetic and browser-served by ruling, so the exposure is not the risk; the risk is an unprotected credential-shaped file in a public repo. This is precisely the file class AC-6's missing guard would catch.

items.title: feat: anomaly detection pipeline, tests, and benchmark (#2)
items.body:
Closes #2

Implements the `detect_anomalies(events) -> list[Anomaly]` seam, a JSONL loader with dead-letter handling, a thin CLI census wrapper, a full unittest suite against `fixtures/event_sample.jsonl`, and a real local benchmark artifact. Builds on the fixture forensics catalog from #1 (`docs/fixture-forensics.md`).

## What changed

### Core pipeline (`src/analytics_pipeline/`)

- **`anomalies.py`** — `detect_anomalies` scans events for all nine data-quality classes from the corrected taxonomy (duplicate `event_id`, clock skew, timezone offset, future timestamp, missing required field, unexpected PII, schema drift, bot burst) plus `compliance_critical` for `privacy_request` events. Each finding is an `Anomaly` dataclass with `event_id`, `anomaly_class`, `detail`, and `action` (`dedupe`, `flag_for_correction`, `normalize`, `quarantine`, `route_compliance`). Timestamp classification uses signal-based heuristics (documented in `docs/adr/0001-timestamp-anomaly-classification-by-signal-not-id.md`), not hard-coded event IDs.
- **`loader.py`** — `load_jsonl` parses JSONL line-by-line; malformed lines (e.g. `evt-0020` on line 21) are dead-lettered with extracted `event_id` instead of crashing the pipeline.
- **`main.py`** — CLI (`python -m analytics_pipeline.main --fixture …`) loads the fixture, runs detection, and prints a JSON census keyed by `event_id` with per-event status (`clean` / `flagged` / `dead_letter`) and summary counts.

### Tests (`tests/`)

26 unittest cases across three modules:

| Module | Coverage |
|--------|----------|
| `test_anomalies.py` | One test per confirmed anomaly class (9 taxonomy + `compliance_critical`), clean negative (`evt-0001`), all six borderline cases from forensics handoff, census class-presence check |
| `test_loader.py` | Fixture SHA-256 provenance, 24 parseable records, dead-letter for `evt-0020`, fallback `event_id` for unparseable lines |
| `test_main.py` | Census shape (24 keys), forensics-aligned summary counts (11 clean / 12 flagged / 1 dead letter), CLI subprocess smoke test |

### Benchmark (`scripts/benchmark.py`, `docs/benchmark-results.md`)

- Runs 10,000 iterations of `detect_anomalies` against the full fixture.
- Verifies fixture SHA-256 (`1aeb24b4…`) before benchmarking; fails fast on fixture rotation.
- Writes `docs/benchmark-results.md` with `[Benchmarked]` throughput/latency and `[Observed]` pass/fail census counts per SCORING.md evidence tiers.

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] `detect_anomalies(events) -> list[Anomaly]` implemented as the single seam (Python 3.11 stdlib only)
- [x] Thin CLI wrapper reads the fixture and serializes results keyed by `event_id`
- [x] Malformed `evt-0020` line dead-lettered without crashing
- [x] unittest suite: one test per confirmed class, one clean case, one test per borderline case
- [x] Full test suite passes against the real fixture (26/26)
- [x] Local benchmark executed with raw timing and pass/fail counts captured

## Test plan

- [x] `python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -v` — 26 tests, all OK
- [x] `PYTHONPATH=src python3 -m analytics_pipeline.main --fixture fixtures/event_sample.jsonl` — JSON census with 24 keys, summary `clean=11`, `flagged=12`, `dead_letter=1`
- [x] `python3 scripts/benchmark.py` — updates `docs/benchmark-results.md` with checksum, ~0.11 ms mean latency, ~212k events/sec throughput
- [x] `shasum -a 256 fixtures/event_sample.jsonl` — matches forensics catalog checksum

items.body:
## What this changes, and why

Storing benchmark results in the repository was the wrong model.
`benchmarks/results/*.jsonl` fed Docusaurus charts, and keeping that dataset
honest grew an apparatus around it — publication gating, record comparators,
rig-selection machinery — that cost more than the answers it produced. A
wall-clock figure is only meaningful beside the branch it is compared with, on
hardware quiet enough to compare on. This retires the standing suite rather than
maintaining a published table nothing re-measures.

Four commits, ordered so the tree stays coherent:

1. **`docs(spate-core,ci)`** — relocation first, so the next commit is purely
   subtractive. The bench-authoring conventions, the pinned-corpus rule, the
   pairing between a wall-clock case and its counted sibling, and the
   operator-chain design claim move into the CI reference's § Performance gates,
   beside the jobs that keep them true.
2. **`docs(spate,spate-json,spate-kafka,spate-clickhouse,docs,website)`** —
   delete `docs/benchmarks/`, `website/plugins/benchmark-results/` and
   `website/src/components/Bench/`, with the sidebar category, the
   `/docs/BENCHMARKS` redirect, the plugin registration, the
   `sidebarItemsGenerator` override and the navbar/footer entries. Atomic: the
   site build is green only when all of that moves together.
3. **`build(benchmarks,workspace)`** — drop the `benchmarks` crate and the
   workspace-level exemptions it earned.
4. **`ci`** — remove the `synthetic-trend` job, the `--exclude benchmarks`
   rustdoc flag, the `/benchmarks/` coverage regexes, the `benchmarks/results/*`
   classifier arm and `make bench-ab`.

Every reference into the deleted pages is resolved rather than retargeted,
including the ones `onBrokenLinks` cannot see — bare prose naming "the benchmark
pages", crate doc comments and `Cargo.toml` comments citing a study by name.

## The gungraun tier is untouched

`crates/*/benches/*_gungraun.rs`, `bench_seams`, `scripts/gungraun-*.sh`, the
`perf-*` jobs, the `ci: bench` label and `[profile.bench]` are all unchanged.
`scripts/gungraun-benches.sh` prints a **byte-identical** 15-target discovery
list before and after this branch, verified by `diff` against a clean checkout of
`main`. The criterion and divan targets under each crate stay, and
`make bench-check` still compiles them in the release profile.

## What six review rounds changed, and what still needs a human eye

Six independent adversarial reviews ran against this branch. **The structural
removal survived all six untouched** — no dangling reference, no broken build,
no workspace inconsistency, and `scripts/gungraun-benches.sh` prints a
byte-identical 15-target list against `main` every time.

Every defect any round found was in the **replacement prose**, and in four
consecutive rounds the worst finding was created by the previous round's *fix*.
That is worth stating plainly rather than burying: the risky part of this change
was never the deletion, it was rewriting sentences whose supporting data the
same commit removes.

The final batch therefore contains **no rewrites**. Where a sentence was found
wrong, it is reverted to `main`'s wording minus the dead link:

- The chunk-sizing and queue-depth sentences in `05-deployment/tuning.mdx` are
  back to `main`'s. One replacement had invented a recommendation — "the room
  worth using is the range just above the default" — that appears in no source
  and inverts the deleted page's actual conclusion that seal size is not a
  production lever.
- `native-format.mdx`'s saturated-server disclosure is back to `main`'s. The
  replacement claimed the table "does not isolate" a quantity that row 4 of the
  same table measures.
- The simd memcpy figure is **restored**, not paraphrased. Like the Kafka
  prefetch number, it was machine-recorded, so dropping it was the error.

Two corrections were kept because they are simple facts: `docs/DESIGN.md` no
longer says `chain.rs` "hard-asserts" anything (it contains no `assert`; the
gate is `crates/spate-core/tests/chain_alloc.rs`), and the four figures whose
rigs this diff deletes now carry one consistent honest attribution instead of
three `benchmark-verified` labels and one accurate one.

**On the zero-copy figures.** `docs/DESIGN.md` previously validated the seam
with the prototype's ~40 ns/record, whose correction lived only on a page this
diff deletes. Two reviewers independently re-ran `cargo bench -p spate-core
--bench chain`: the borrowed arm emits a record roughly every 10 ns with **7
allocations per batch**, the owned arm **519 per 512 records**. The page now
claims only the allocation contrast, because the arms fan out differently
(`flat_map` into three sub-records against `map` into one, with divan counters
to match) — a cross-arm wall-clock ratio is not a quantity that rig produces,
and the old page's 2.5× was that artifact.
## A dependency-resolution gap closes as a side effect

The `lz4_flex` workspace entry carried default features and unified them onto the
copy the ClickHouse client pulls. A workspace build therefore compressed through
`lz4_flex`'s safe, checked paths while everything resolved from
`spate-clickhouse` — every actual consumer — used the unchecked ones: CI was
exercising code nobody runs. Both sides now resolve the same feature set, and
what `-p spate-clickhouse` resolves is unchanged from `main`.

## Size

13,399 lines are whole-file deletion across 65 files and need no line-by-line
reading. The judged part is ~470 changed lines across ~40 files — that is the
half worth reviewing.

## Changelog

No fragment and no `Changelog: none` trailer. Two commits do name crate scopes,
so the exemption is earned by **type** rather than by scope: `docs` is not one of
the types that requires a fragment, and `build(benchmarks,workspace)` names only
non-crate areas. Nothing published changes — no crate's API, features or resolved
dependency graph moves for a consumer, and `THIRD-PARTY.md` regenerates
byte-identically. `Changelog: none` is reserved for a fix to a bug that was never
released, which this is not. `make check-changelog` agrees.

## Known and deliberate

- The `benchmarks` commit scope and the `area: benchmarks` label keep their
  names, and the label loses its labeler path rule — leaving it the one `area:`
  label without a trigger. Both are revisited by the harness pull request that
  introduces the replacement `bench` crate, where a rename can be made in one
  place alongside the thing it names. Seven open issues carry the label.
- Five of those seven (#89, #84, #83, #82, #62) are bug reports against rigs this
  branch deletes. They become unactionable on merge and want closing or
  transferring — a maintainer call, not made here.
- The 13 published `/docs/benchmarks/*` URLs 404 after the next deploy. No
  redirect is added: the plugin's own comment records the precedent for a
  *deleted* page (the avro `fast-backend` entry went when that backend did), and
  a redirect needs a `to` that exists.
- Pre-existing and left alone: `make self-test` and `make check-features` cannot
  run concurrently (`cargo hack --no-dev-deps` rewrites manifests under
  `cargo metadata`'s feet), which makes a green branch look red to anyone
  reproducing these gates in parallel.

## Invariants

None touched. Every change under `crates/` is a comment: `git diff main...HEAD --
'crates/**/*.rs'` filtered of comment and blank lines is empty.

- [ ] **INV-1** · [ ] **INV-2** · [ ] **INV-3** · [ ] **INV-4** · [ ] **INV-5**
- [ ] **INV-6** · [ ] **INV-7** · [ ] **INV-8** · [ ] **INV-9** · [ ] **INV-10**

## Semver

- [x] Additive — nothing existing changes
- [ ] Breaking

## Checks

Ticked by exit code, on a quiet machine.

- [x] `make gates`
- [x] `make docs` — `CI=true` via the Makefile, so redirect validation ran; no
      anchor warnings in the log
- [x] Any ad-hoc cargo command run with `--locked`
- [x] `make attribution` — `THIRD-PARTY.md` regenerates byte-identically
- [x] Conventional Commits, scoped to the areas touched, no AI attribution
- [x] Changelog: exempt, for the reason above

Also run individually, each checked by exit code: `cargo metadata --locked`,
`make self-test`, `check-invariants`, `check-labels`, `check-changelog`,
`check-gungraun-benches`, `check-collected-region`, `check-perf-report`,
`shellcheck`, `make zizmor`, `actionlint .github/workflows/*.yml`,
`scripts/gungraun-benches.sh --self-test`, `make bench-gungraun-check`,
`make bench-check`, and `cargo doc --workspace --no-deps --all-features --locked`.

Not run, and why: `make loom` (no sync code changed) and `make bench-gungraun`
(needs Linux and valgrind; the tier is instead proven byte-identical to `main`).
A reviewer ran `make test-docker` green.

items.title: Re-gauge the eight-record quality gates, and fix TFG's
items.body:
The sentinels in each simulator are fitted by one rule -- worst observed
across the eight scored records plus about half a percent, rounded up to the
next tenth -- and the rule only means anything if it is re-applied after the
filter changes. Re-applied here to all five families that score those records.

Four were already at the rule and are untouched: OU-II, OU-III, NLO and the
PII observer each sit within a tenth of what the filter now produces, so
every gate value in them is left exactly as it stands.

TFG's were not. All seven were fitted before the adaptation-policy work that
brought its orchestrator up to OU-III's -- commit timing, the 0.1 s schedule
tick, the r_S floor from 0.4 to 0.15, the tau-scaled S=0 cadence -- and were
never revisited, so every bar carried slack a regression could hide in. The
worst case is the horizontal channel: 3D error on PM-Stokes is 25.78% against
a bar of 68.0, and on JONSWAP 20.99% against 30.6. All seven come down.

That also retires half of a standing finding. The note in the simulator said
3D error degrades sharply on the large-wave records; it did, in the filter
those bars were fitted to, and it does not now -- JONSWAP 3D lands exactly on
OU-III's own bar. What remains is accelerometer bias, still four times
OU-III's and above 100% of the true bias on six of eight records, and yaw,
which is three times OU-III's because the continuous hard-iron correction is
an OU-III component this filter does not carry. Both stay recorded rather
than endorsed.

bias_3d_percent still gates the gyro channel behind the accelerometer's much
larger number on every family. Splitting them means changing W3dFailureLimits
for all of them and is deliberately not done here.

docs/quality-gate-regauge.md has the measured worst value behind every gate
in all five families, and how to reproduce them.

items.title: chore(docs): remove the internal benchmarks and manuals, and correct the offload figures
items.body:
## Description

Most of what is removed here already has a counterpart upstream in the backend repo and will
arrive through the backend sync. What lives in this repo today is a second, hand-maintained
copy, so the two drift apart. Dropping them leaves a single source.

| This repo (removed) | backend counterpart |
|---|---|
| `backend/tests/benchmark_llama_server_prefill.py` | `tests/e2e/benchmark_llama_server_prefill.py` |
| `backend/tests/benchmark_offload_vram.py` | `tests/e2e/benchmark_offload_vram.py` |
| `docs/benchmarks.md` (zh) · `docs/benchmarks.en.md` | `docs/benchmarks.md` (en) |
| `docs/inference_manual.html` (zh) · `.en.html` | `docs/inference_manual.zh-TW.html` · `inference_manual.html` |
| `docs/finetune_manual.html` (zh) · `.en.html` | `docs/finetune_manual.zh-TW.html` · `finetune_manual.html` |
| `docs/site-map.html` | `docs/site-map.html` |

Note the language-suffix convention is **inverted** between the two repos: here the bare
`.html` / `.md` is the Traditional Chinese file and `.en` marks English, while upstream the
bare name is English and `.zh-TW` marks Chinese. The names collide but the languages do not
line up, so the sync needs to account for it rather than assume a same-name overwrite.

Three things have no upstream counterpart and are simply dropped:

- The two raw result files, `benchmark_llama_server_prefill_results.json` and
  `benchmark_offload_vram_results.json`. Upstream deliberately keeps benchmark output out of
  git (`chore(tests): keep the llama-server benchmark results out of git`) and writes it to a
  gitignored `tests/results/` instead. This repo now matches that.
- The three example configs: `examples/fine-tune_configs/Llama3.3-70B-finetune.json`,
  `examples/fine-tune_configs/qwen3.5-122b-lora-finetune.json`, and
  `examples/inference_configs/GPT-OSS-120B-demo-inference.json`. These were written here and
  exist nowhere else, so they go away rather than moving. The `examples/` directory is emptied
  and disappears.

**References updated:**

- `README.md` / `README.zh-TW.md` — drop the links and directory entries pointing at
  benchmarks, the site map, both HTML manuals, and `examples/`.
- `wiki/{en,zh}/comparisons/trusta-ast-vs-market-solutions.md`,
  `concepts/offload-mechanism.md`, `summary/trusta-ast-core-differentiation.md` — replace
  "see `benchmark_*.py` / reproduce it with that script / raw data in `*_results.json`" with
  "measured in-house". Those paths were already stale once upstream moved `tests/` to
  `tests/e2e/`; naming no path means a future upstream reorganisation cannot rot these pages
  again.

## Corrected figure

The published VRAM reduction was wrong and is corrected here, in
`wiki/{en,zh}/concepts/offload-mechanism.md` and
`wiki/{en,zh}/summary/trusta-ast-core-differentiation.md`.

The old figure compared whole-device VRAM against model weights. The device peak includes
whatever other processes were already holding, and the benchmark recorded that baseline
without ever subtracting it, so the reduction was understated. The backend PR fixes the
benchmark; this applies the same correction to what is already published:

    model peak = 13.39 - 1.65 = 11.74 GB
    reduction  = 1 - 11.74 / 27.508 = 57.3%        (was published as 51.3%)

This is **recomputed from the raw fields the original run recorded, not a new run**. The
full-GPU requirement, the pre-load baseline and the device peak were all captured correctly;
only the final arithmetic was wrong. The pages now state both numbers — the ~11.7 GB
attributable to the model and the ~13.4 GB the device actually peaked at — so the two are no
longer conflated.

**The tok/s figure is deliberately left at ~0.5 and flagged as pending.** The original run
stored a count of SSE chunks in the `completion_tokens` field, so the real token count was
never recorded and cannot be recovered. Confirming it needs the benchmark re-run against a GPU
with the weights available.

## Related Issues

<!-- e.g. Closes #123, Relates to #456 -->

## Checklist

- [x] The PR title follows [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/en/v1.0.0/)
- [x] Commits follow Conventional Commits (see [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md))
- [ ] `pytest` passes locally — not run; no collected test was touched (`backend/pytest.ini`
      sets no `python_files`, so `benchmark_*.py` was never collected)
- [x] Tests were added or updated where relevant — n/a, deletions and documentation only
- [x] Documentation was updated where relevant (English and 繁體中文 where applicable)
- [x] I have read the [Code of Conduct](CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md)

## Notes for Reviewers

- **Merge order matters.** `benchmark_offload_vram.py` only exists upstream once the
  corresponding backend PR lands — it is added there in the same change that fixes the
  hard-coded paths. Merge that one first, or this table describes a file that is not there yet.
- The corrected reduction is arithmetic on already-recorded measurements, so it needs no GPU to
  verify: the three inputs are in the deleted `benchmark_offload_vram_results.json`, visible in
  this PR's diff.
- Every deleted filename was grepped across the repo; nothing links to them any more. The only
  remaining mentions are provenance notes in `wiki/{en,zh}/log.md` and
  `wiki/{en,zh}/sources/finetune_manual.md` ("Ingested `inference_manual.html`"), which record
  where the wiki content came from rather than linking to the file, so they were left as they
  are.
- The HTML manuals' content was already absorbed into `wiki/{en,zh}/sources/`; the wiki itself
  is untouched.

items.title: docs: first full benchmark sweep with results and limitations
items.body:
﻿## Summary

First full sweep of the matrix: **23 measured runs across five runtimes**, ~35 minutes, written up in `docs/12-benchmark-report.md`.

- `scripts/run-benchmarks.ps1` — one target at a time (no JVM competing with another for host CPU), a discarded warmup per cell, N reps, fresh container per target. Reads orchestrator Basic auth from `.env`.
- `scripts/analyze-benchmarks.mjs` — per-cell **medians** (not means; one slow rep would skew a mean at n=3).
- Report includes method, results, four findings, and an explicit section on what the data does *not* support.

## Findings

| | Result |
| :-- | :-- |
| Java 8 tail latency | p95 **17.8 ms** vs 2.9–5.9 ms elsewhere, reproducible across reps (64.6 / 17.8 / 17.7) |
| Virtual threads, OS threads | **22 vs 31**, identical in every rep, zero variance |
| Virtual threads, memory | **+15 MB RSS**, −7 MB Java heap — no memory win at this scale |
| Throughput | Flat 39.7–44.8 rps everywhere: the load is self-paced, so these are cost figures, not capacity |

## Correction

`docs/01 §4.2` previously claimed, from one ad-hoc run, that virtual threads saved ~55 MB. Three reps show the opposite. The original compared a container that had been up for hours against a freshly started one. Corrected in place with a note, since it was a quotable number in the repo.

## Honesty notes in the report

- Only the Java 21 pair varies one variable; Java 8 vs 21 also changes the Spring shell, and Java 11/17 have larger cgroups.
- One SSE context-switch cell reads 117,698/s — that is one wild rep (1,895 and 233,500, n=2 so median = mean), flagged as an artifact rather than a finding.
- JFR aggregates are `jfr print` line counts, not parsed events; the platform-vs-virtual park gap is partly an instrumentation difference.
- `scripts/bench-manifest.json` is gitignored — it indexes run artifacts that are themselves gitignored.

items.title: ConvRot: documentation additions and corrections (group size should be 256)

This pull request updates the experimental ConvRot documentation in all supported languages to clarify loader compatibility, recommend a new default Hadamard group size, and add real-world training benchmarks. The most important changes are grouped below.

**Loader and Quantization Path Clarifications**
* All docs now clarify that `SimpleTuner` does not consume arbitrary ConvRot sidecar buffers as a standalone feature, but supports compatible single-file INT8 ConvRot transformer safetensors via SDNQ Hadamard if the loader supports it. [[1]](diffhunk://#diff-8558ca2d92b0c8f908e32e16d9fdad4b57bc017287bd6333df78702d8e2c2c2dL5-R5) [[2]](diffhunk://#diff-e6428317e0316c2e6bbd50d10b7425b859dc97242598c9bcd6fa473423cc2450L5-R5) [[3]](diffhunk://#diff-92fa37945f98d1e6ac1ce6cc3197d444f5f634e9671118a635b1680e57218a27L5-R5) [[4]](diffhunk://#diff-d46f6ea4e5745e3f0cdeac35434200525f41ccb734088128a99b1c118c9e9b04L5-R5) [[5]](diffhunk://#diff-b7c365c71e8d13e57492291d6f1232b980e878dab2f84948778b89b3b6856c1bL5-R5)

**Configuration Recommendations**
* The recommended default for `sdnq_hadamard_group_size` is changed from `128` to `256` in both code snippets and option explanations, with notes that smaller blocks select a QuaRot-style path. [[1]](diffhunk://#diff-8558ca2d92b0c8f908e32e16d9fdad4b57bc017287bd6333df78702d8e2c2c2dL14-R14) [[2]](diffhunk://#diff-8558ca2d92b0c8f908e32e16d9fdad4b57bc017287bd6333df78702d8e2c2c2dL27-R27) [[3]](diffhunk://#diff-92fa37945f98d1e6ac1ce6cc3197d444f5f634e9671118a635b1680e57218a27L14-R14) [[4]](diffhunk://#diff-92fa37945f98d1e6ac1ce6cc3197d444f5f634e9671118a635b1680e57218a27L27-R27) [[5]](diffhunk://#diff-d46f6ea4e5745e3f0cdeac35434200525f41ccb734088128a99b1c118c9e9b04L14-R14) [[6]](diffhunk://#diff-d46f6ea4e5745e3f0cdeac35434200525f41ccb734088128a99b1c118c9e9b04L27-R27) [[7]](diffhunk://#diff-b7c365c71e8d13e57492291d6f1232b980e878dab2f84948778b89b3b6856c1bL14-R14) [[8]](diffhunk://#diff-b7c365c71e8d13e57492291d6f1232b980e878dab2f84948778b89b3b6856c1bL27-R27)

**Requirements and Dependency Handling**
* Documentation now states that `SimpleTuner` installs and configures the SDNQ training dependency automatically for supported install targets, replacing the prior manual SDNQ build instructions. [[1]](diffhunk://#diff-8558ca2d92b0c8f908e32e16d9fdad4b57bc017287bd6333df78702d8e2c2c2dL41-R62) [[2]](diffhunk://#diff-92fa37945f98d1e6ac1ce6cc3197d444f5f634e9671118a635b1680e57218a27L41-R62) [[3]](diffhunk://#diff-d46f6ea4e5745e3f0cdeac35434200525f41ccb734088128a99b1c118c9e9b04L41-R62) [[4]](diffhunk://#diff-b7c365c71e8d13e57492291d6f1232b980e878dab2f84948778b89b3b6856c1bL41-R62)

**Quantization Guidance and Caveats**
* New warnings are added that ConvRot can reduce quantization damage, but INT8 performance is not guaranteed to match BF16/FP8 for all models; users are advised to validate loss curves and generated samples before long training runs. [[1]](diffhunk://#diff-8558ca2d92b0c8f908e32e16d9fdad4b57bc017287bd6333df78702d8e2c2c2dL41-R62) [[2]](diffhunk://#diff-92fa37945f98d1e6ac1ce6cc3197d444f5f634e9671118a635b1680e57218a27L41-R62) [[3]](diffhunk://#diff-d46f6ea4e5745e3f0cdeac35434200525f41ccb734088128a99b1c118c9e9b04L41-R62) [[4]](diffhunk://#diff-b7c365c71e8d13e57492291d6f1232b980e878dab2f84948778b89b3b6856c1bL41-R62)

**Benchmark Results**

items.title: feat: score corrected transcripts and republish WER
items.body:
## Context

Every published number in this repository measures raw ASR output or
diarization. Nothing measures the correction lane — the lane that is the
product's actual review path: the operator supplies a terminology list and the
model repairs the transcript against it, with no human editing pass. There was
no way to answer "did correction help, and did it break anything".

Building that measurement surfaced a metric bug that had to be fixed first, and
fixing it moves two published numbers.

**The normalization bug.** `docs/contracts/scoring.md` declares punctuation
*removal*; `metrics.py` replaced punctuation with *spaces*. Reference `dont` vs
hypothesis `don't` therefore normalized to `dont` vs `don t` — one substitution
plus one insertion, WER 2.0 instead of 0. Correction routinely rewrites
punctuation, so scoring corrected text under the old normalizer would count
punctuation edits as word errors. The contract was right; the code was wrong.

**Republication (maintainer-approved 2026-08-11).** Fixing it changes WER only —
CER is mathematically invariant because character scoring strips all whitespace
after normalization:

| Published value | Before | After |
|---|---:|---:|
| Korean VibeVoice WER | 0.128 | 0.141 |
| Italian MOSS WER | 0.081 | 0.085 |
| All CER values | unchanged | unchanged |

Term recall, omissions, and backchannel 7/7 do not move.

## Changes

- **`metrics.py`** deletes punctuation instead of replacing it with spaces, per
  the declared contract. Apostrophe (ASCII and typographic), hyphen, NFKC,
  case, whitespace, and Italian-diacritic behavior are pinned by tests.
- **`score.py`** opens its output exclusive-create; an existing scores artifact
  is preserved instead of truncated (judgment rule 3: artifacts are
  create-only).
- **Republication in the same change**: `benchmarks/published-results.json`
  (with fresh artifact SHA-256 provenance), all ten READMEs, the four generated
  figures, both historical verdict docs, the app profile resource and the app
  test that pins those values, and a new `D36 [maintainer]` decision record in
  `PROJECT.md`.
- **`score_corrected.py`** (new): scores a correction run's raw and corrected
  output against one reference. Before trusting any number it verifies the
  correction respected the contract — segment count, speakers, timestamps,
  source, language, confidence all unchanged — and rejects with the offending
  segment and field named. Reports per-metric directional deltas,
  applied-vs-review counts, and correction-safety classification.
- **Correction-safety counting**: an applied change is evaluated only when
  exactly one reference segment has the identical time interval; raw and
  corrected CER/WER edit counts are then compared Pareto-style (`closer`,
  `further`, `mixed`, `unchanged`, plus `correct_to_incorrect` when a correct
  segment was rewritten wrong). If any applied change cannot be aligned,
  `correction_made_worse_count` is `null` rather than a misleading zero, with
  the observed count and unevaluated list alongside.
- **`compare_correction_paths.py`** (new): the four-state harness — no-glossary
  ASR, decode-time glossary ASR, each corrected — emitting one create-only
  verdict JSON with the three deltas that matter: decode-time injection gain,
  correction gain, correction gain without decode-time injection. Thresholds
  live in a versioned JSON file; every value is deliberately `null` and the
  verdict stays `passed: null` until the maintainer sets standards.

## Validation

- Scoring suite: **69/69** (baseline before the change: 49/49, zero failures).
- Contract checker: all three schemas pass.
- README checker: all ten files match the declaration.
- Figure suite: 6/6 after regenerating the four SVGs.
- `swift build` passes; the app test target passes **45 tests in 7 suites**
  after updating the two pinned WER values.
- Red-then-green evidence recorded for the normalizer fix (4 failures before),
  the corrected scorer, and the harness.
- A synthetic four-state demonstration produces the expected deltas, including
  one deliberate `correct_to_incorrect` regression caught by the safety count.

Not verified: a live correction turn against a real model — the harness
consumes completed run directories and this host has no pinned model caches.
The fixture demonstration covers the tooling, not model behavior.

## Notes for review

- `Tests/MaccheroniAppTests/AppShellTests.swift` is also touched by #9 in a
  different region; whichever merges second rebases trivially.
- A follow-up contract doc should specify the corrected-score JSON shape and
  the four-state verdict semantics; flagged in the report rather than edited,
  since `docs/contracts/` changes deserve their own review.
- The threshold placeholders in
  `benchmarks/scripts/scoring/correction-comparison-thresholds.json` are yours
  to set; the harness reports `not_configured` until then.

items.title: docs: re-measure the cross-engine table on current main (#348)
items.body:
Fixes #348.

## Why

The published cross-engine table was committed **2026-08-02 12:53**. Column projection merged at **17:33** the same day. Every figure in it came from a build where the reader decoded every column of every row group regardless of the query (#338).

It understated the project, which is the direction nobody audits:

| | published | measured today |
|---|---|---|
| q6 pgColumnar | 81,966 ms | **1,592 ms** |
| q6 TimescaleDB | 1,771 ms | 6,956 ms |
| q4, q5 | pgColumnar loses to heap | does not reproduce |

## Why it is a new run, not a line-by-line correction

Two things make a row-by-row edit misleading:

- **The fixture changed.** Both tables now carry a `(hostname, time DESC)` btree. Heap goes from 11,045 ms to **6 ms** on q1, a factor of ~1,800. That is not drift.
- **The old queries were never recorded**, and `bench-tsdb/BENCHMARK_RESULTS.md`, cited by #289 as "full data + method", has never existed in this repository.

So the method is stated and **the SQL is published with the table**, which is the main thing the old one lacked.

## q1 to q3 ship with their cause attached

They cost ~28.7 ms **per row returned**, flat across a twelve-fold change in row count, on the same `Index Scan` plan heap uses. That is #353 (default `stripe_row_limit` over the 32 MB fetch cache), compounded by #355 (planner takes an index scan for ordering without modelling fetch cost).

Publishing q2 at 123 seconds without that would read as a property of columnar storage. It is one default and one cost model, and the doc says so, with the workaround.

## TimescaleDB is serial and labelled

Its parallel path fails on the bench host with `could not read blocks 0..0`. **Not caused by pgColumnar**: it persists with every pgColumnar planner hook disabled, and the chunks use the heap AM. Neither workaround is usable, one still errors and the other silently returns zero rows.

Citus is omitted rather than carried forward from an unknown configuration.

## Storage table unchanged

Measured 6,587 MB / 7,975 MB / 22 GB against its published 6.4 / 7.8 / 22 GB. **It was correct.** #348 originally suspected it; that suspicion is withdrawn. The 2.67 GB figure in #289's body was the wrong one.

## Correctness

Verified per query against heap. Counts and `max` match exactly. Averages agree to 2.9e-15 relative difference, the residual being float reassociation across workers. No group appears in one engine and not the other.

An earlier md5-based check appeared to show q4, q5 and q6 mismatching. That was the instrument: md5 over the text of `avg()` output changes on the last digit. Recorded so it is not rediscovered.

## Gate

`docs_style` passes. The STE line-length rule required splitting several sentences.
